entry.title: Shentu v0.5.3
entry.content:
• A proposal button pressed always gets an answer (#163): it says at once that it checks the address again, the log notes the press (proposal_press) before the checks, the checks run within a minute and past it the press is refused with the gate's word, and a failure inside is answered and logged. As before, a pressed button is used up whatever follows: one refused because its checks ran out of time, failed or were cut by a restart cannot be pressed again, and the next check's buttons are the ones to use.
  • Telegram blocks ask only what the gate would allow (#155, #158): from a chat channel, block_ip runs the checks of #108's gate before asking for ✅. An address the gate refuses is refused at once, with no ✅ to press; the agent is told the gate's fixed word (and the address), and the gate's own message stays in the server's log only. When the block itself fails after the confirmation, its error too stays in the log only. Confirmed blocks are checked again when they run, as before.
  • While the bot waits (#156, #158): a message sent meanwhile is told what it waits for (the ✅ above, the authenticator code, or the server's approval with sudo shentu bot approve) instead of "Still working"; a question sent meanwhile is not passed to the agent (the authenticator code and the commands /lockdown, /new, /usage and /attacks still work). A proposal or suggestion button pressed meanwhile stays, to be pressed again later; a suggestion is no longer used up.
  • shentu dispatch (#158): wrong arguments get the usage first, before the configuration is read and whoever runs it; stats and repair then ask for root (an elevated prompt on Windows). sudo shentu dispatch repair keeps each broken line in *.jsonl.bad once, and the daily report says how many moved lines were new to it.
  • Next 15: const h = await headers(); h.get(name) and the sync const h = headers() are read as headers().get(name) in a file that imports next/headers, so a Host header read this way and passed to a redirect is reported by js-open-redirect-next (and by the SSRF and command injection rules that read headers()) (#157).
  • Koa: a middleware a Koa application or router registers with use is followed through destructuring and aliases of its context, as a route handler is (app.use(async (ctx) => { const { host } = ctx.request.headers; ... })), when the function uses its first parameter as a context. An HTTP client's interceptor or a library's plugin registered with use is not read as one (#157).
  • Laravel: $request->sort, a magic property, and the closure of ->when($request->input('sort'), fn ($q, $s) => $q->orderBy($s)) (and ->unless) are read by php-sqli-orderby-identifier, where $request may be Laravel's request: the file uses a class of Illuminate, declares it with a Request type, or holds a class extending a Controller, or, in a project using Illuminate, it is a function's untyped parameter (#157).
  • SSRF: the check of a URL's host is no longer kept at console.log(u), JSON.stringify(u) or String(u) in a file that may replace them unseen in more ways: Function as a value, Function.prototype.bind, getPrototypeOf, Reflect.construct, vm's runners, GLOBAL, top, this other than read through a named member, the console module required or imported, and a require( or import( of anything but a plain string, or createRequire (#157).
  • Files with any of the patterns above report an SSRF finding again at fetch(u) after console.log(u), as before v0.4.3. With the new Next, Koa and Laravel reads, the routes attack detection takes as reachable may change.
  • A data object whose type name ends in Request (SearchRequest $request) is read as Laravel's request, as a FormRequest is.
  • Next's headers() is followed only in a file that imports next/headers itself.
  • in_array($request->query('s'), [...], true) ? $request->query('s') : null is not taken as a check of the value, with a request call as the source (the same with a magic property is).
  • shentu usage leaves out the model calls of an automatic incident check's sub-agents (sub:incident): on a test server it listed 9 calls where the log held 13. shentu budget counts them. The fix (#164) is planned for v0.5.4.
  • The automatic incident check's notice and the "Approved from Telegram" notice are in English whatever language is set to.

entry.title: Shentu v0.5.2
entry.content:
• The sub-agents' own model (#135): [agents] base_url, model and api_key_env give them a model of their own; unset, they use [llm]. A model outside this host (anything but 127.0.0.0/8, ::1 and localhost) needs [budget] monthly_tokens, or no sub-agent runs and nothing is sent; a dispatch that used one says so to the agent, in the archive and in the daily report. What it is sent is masked as before. From it, an error answer keeps only its status, as its text could quote the key; redirects are not followed, and a request that fails keeps only the kind of failure, not its URL. [llm]'s errors have the key replaced, as is and in its common encodings, before they are cut.
  • Sub-agents at once (#136): on a model outside this host they run together, each with an equal share of the dispatch's token cap, when this month's token limit has room for a whole dispatch and, with monthly_cost set, under half of it is spent. On a model at this host, in any address form, they still take turns.
  • sudo shentu dispatch repair (#134): moves the archive's unreadable lines to <date>.jsonl.bad and drops empty ones, so automatic incident checks resume without waiting up to 72 hours. Files are replaced in one rename, and the archive's lock is dispatch/.lock. On Windows it and dispatch stats run from an elevated prompt; run by anyone else, both say so before reading the configuration.
  • Operator feedback (#137): under a dispatch's report the bot offers 👍 useful and 👎 false positive, once, for 7 days, to the paired user. sudo shentu dispatch stats [--days 7] [--json] adds the numbers up by role and suggests changes within fixed ranges (steps 4 to 10, tokens 20,000 to 60,000, a prompt review). A tool could only ever be suggested away, never added; no tool suggestion is made yet. Shentu applies none itself.
  • Platforms (#138): a role gets only the tools that work on this platform, and the others are listed as unchecked; proposals only on Linux; on macOS only surface runs for now; automatic incident checks run on Linux only and take no daily slot elsewhere.
  • An [agents] model on a LAN address or a host name, Ollama on another machine of the network included, counts as outside this host, and so do 127.1, 0.0.0.0, [::] and this host's own LAN address: set [budget] monthly_tokens.
  • With a costly model, a dispatch's cost can pass half of monthly_cost in one go; the limit stops the next calls, not that one.
  • The bot and the patrol each reserve room for their dispatches without seeing the other's.
  • Automatic incident checks are off on Windows and macOS for now, the incident role included (on Windows it runs with fewer tools and proposes nothing).

entry.title: Shentu v0.5.1
entry.content:
• Dispatch archive (#112): each sub-agent dispatch is saved to state_dir/dispatch/<date>.jsonl (0600 in a 0700 directory, kept 30 days) before its reports go back: roles, statuses and reasons as fixed words, counts, and the proposed addresses in canonical form with what the Telegram gate says of each. No text a sub-agent or a log wrote is kept. Every field is checked when a record is written and when it is read; an archive another user could write, or a link, is not read. The daily report has a section on the last day's dispatches, with addresses masked to /24 (/64 for IPv6).
  • Proposal buttons (#116, #122): after a Telegram answer that dispatched, the bot lists the proposed blocks, with a button for each one that passes the checks block_ip runs from Telegram (#108's gate included) at that moment and was written in canonical form, at most five; any other gets a fixed word for why. A button carries only the dispatch id and a number. Pressing it runs the checks again, then asks for ✅ (with [bot] confirm = 4 too), then blocks. A press is refused for another pairing, after 24 hours, a second time (after a restart too), or when the archive's address differs.
  • Automatic incident checks (#117), off by default ([agents] auto_incident): an L3 group the patrol pushed dispatches the read-only incident sub-agent on its own. One a round, at most 3 a day, a group once a day; none for unverified or overflow groups, none without [budget] monthly_tokens or past 80% of it, and none while the archive or log.jsonl cannot be read to its end. The notice carries fixed words and numbers; its proposals get the same buttons, sent only while the bot service runs and can change the firewall.
  • The bot's and shentu chat's monthly AI budget limit counts a log.jsonl it could not read to its end as used up.
  • Sub-agents still run one after another, and they are built and tested for Linux only.
  • A line cut short in the archive (a full disk, say) stops automatic incident checks for at most 72 hours (usually about two days), until its file is out of the window they read; the daily report says so.
  • With a 7B local model, sub-agents often use up their 6 steps and are reported incomplete.

entry.title: Shentu v0.5.0
entry.content:
• Sub-agents (Linux, one host): in the Telegram bot and shentu chat, the agent can hand read-only checks to up to 3 sub-agents with the dispatch tool, each in one role: patrol, surface, attack or incident (#101). Each role has a fixed list of read-only tools; a sub-agent cannot block or unblock an address, notify, use a skill or dispatch again. They run one after another. Patrol rounds and the eval bot never dispatch.
  • Limits: a sub-agent gets at most 6 model calls, 3 tool calls a step, 2048 output tokens a call, 40,000 tokens and 5 minutes; a dispatch at most 120,000 tokens and 12 minutes, and the monthly budget still applies. Tokens are estimated before each call and counted after it, reasoning tokens included. A sub-agent stopped by a limit, or one that does not answer in the required report, is reported incomplete with the reason, never as done. A model call cut off by a time limit is no longer retried.
  • Reports: each sub-agent answers in a fixed JSON shape (findings, proposals, what it did not check), checked field by field and masked, and the agent reads it marked untrusted. A proposal to block is only a suggestion: after a dispatch, every block_ip or unblock_ip in that conversation asks for the ✅ button even with [bot] confirm = 4, until /new, and its audit log line names the dispatch. The bot's progress message shows the sub-agents' steps (the last 12), and a tool name it does not know as "unknown tool".

entry.title: Shentu v0.4.3
entry.content:
• SSRF: after a URL's host is checked, console.log(u), JSON.stringify(u) or String(u) no longer ends the check, while the file uses console, JSON and String only to call them (no parameter or declaration of those names, no console.log = f) and holds nothing that may replace them unseen (a global object such as globalThis other than read through a named member, eval, Function(, a with statement, anything under a built-in's prototype) (#119).
  • JavaScript route handlers: destructuring with a string key, const { 'x-forwarded-host': xfh } = req.headers, is followed, so the value is reported by js-ssrf-host-header instead of js-ssrf-http-request. In a Koa route handler, a destructured parameter taking request (({ request }) => request.header.host) is read as Koa's context when the file, or another file of the project, imports koa, @koa/router or koa-router (#119).
  • New sources: Next 15's (await headers()).get(...), so a Host header read that way and passed to a redirect is reported by js-open-redirect-next; Laravel's Request::query( and Request::get( in php-sqli-orderby-identifier (DB::raw, ->orderBy() (#118).
  • NestJS: a field of a whole @Headers() object written into a response (h['x-note'] in res.send() is reported by js-xss-response (#125).
  • Duplicate reports removed. One call, one SQL injection rule: where two rules report the same call on the same line, one of them leaves it to the other (yields_to). ->where( with Symfony's $request->query->get( is php-sqli-doctrine-query-text's, no longer also php-sqli-drupal-db-query's; DB::raw(...) inside one of php-sqli-laravel-raw's calls is laravel-raw's where laravel-raw reports it. Another call on the same line is still reported (#125). And in the SSRF rules, after const x = h where h is a whole NestJS @Headers() object or Express's r.headers, x.host (also x['Host'], x['x-forwarded-host']) is reported by js-ssrf-host-header alone, no longer by js-ssrf-http-request too; a name that may also hold another value of the request (r.query on one branch) is still reported by both (#132).
  • Some findings move to another rule: sa.text(...) built from request input is reported by python-sqli-sqlalchemy-text instead of python-sqli-dbapi-format (#118); a string-key destructuring of a Host header by js-ssrf-host-header instead of js-ssrf-http-request (#119); and a call two SQL injection rules reported is reported once (#125). php-sqli-laravel-raw's fix now says an ORDER BY column or direction needs an allowlist. With them, the routes attack detection takes as reachable may change.
  • A Koa middleware registered with app.use is not a route handler: its context is followed only as written (ctx.request.headers['x-forwarded-host']), not through destructuring (const { host } = ctx.request.headers) or an alias (const h = ctx.request.headers).
  • A name reassigned on every branch is still followed after them, which reports more than it must.
  • Next 15's const h = await headers(); h.get(name) and the sync h = headers() are not sources yet.
  • The JavaScript read-only calls do not yet see Object.getPrototypeOf, an alias of Function, Reflect.construct, vm.compileFunction, or a global object reached through this, GLOBAL or top; and typeof window sends the whole file back to ending the check at console.log(u).

entry.title: Shentu v0.4.2
entry.content:
• The JavaScript rules follow a route handler's request whatever it is called: a parameter not named req ((r, s) =>), a Koa context not named ctx, an alias (const q = r, const h = r.headers) and destructuring (({ headers }, res) =>, const { headers, hostname: hn } = r, const { host } = req.headers). So r.hostname, r.get('host'), c.host and a destructured headers are reported now; a Host header read this way goes to js-ssrf-host-header, other headers to js-ssrf-http-request. A request header index is read in lower case, as Node stores it (r.headers['Host']). In the SSRF rules, Koa's ctx.header and ctx.request.get( are sources too, and so are ctx.request.header.host and ctx.request.headers.host for the Host header (#106).
  • NestJS: @Request() counts as the handler's request, as @Req() does, in the 13 JavaScript rules that read @Req() (SSRF, SQL and NoSQL injection, command injection, code evaluation, path traversal, LDAP injection, deserialization). Both count as NestJS's only when the file, or another file of the project, imports @nestjs/common or @nestjs/core; elsewhere they are an object like any other (#103, #106).
  • Python: global and nonlocal continued with a backslash are read to the end of the statement, so a name on the next line is declared too (#103).
  • SSRF: after a URL's host is checked, a = u.valueOf() followed by a change to a, or a method of u called by a computed name (u['valueOf'](), u[k](...)), ends the check, as a = u does (#103).
  • A web log owned by the server's own account no longer backs a block when systemd's userdb directories (/etc/userdb, /run/userdb, /run/host/userdb, /usr/local/lib/userdb, /usr/lib/userdb) hold any entry or cannot be read: userdb can add accounts and group memberships that /etc/passwd and /etc/group do not show (#113).
  • Hardening only: the block check also reads an address in an inet_aton form (3405803788, 0xcb.0.113.12, ...), and the block check and campaigns read ::ffff:a.b.c.d as a.b.c.d. Access logs never yield these forms (since v0.4.0 a client must be a plain address, and ::ffff: is read as IPv4), so nothing changes in practice (#113, #124).
  • Some JavaScript findings move to another rule: a Host header read as r.headers['X-Forwarded-Host'] or const { host } = req.headers is reported by js-ssrf-host-header instead of js-ssrf-http-request; @Req() in a project that does not import NestJS is reported by js-ssrf-http-request; const { host } = req.headers written into a response is no longer reported by js-xss-response, as Host has not been XSS input since v0.4.1. With them, the routes attack detection takes as reachable may change.
  • On a host whose systemd userdb directories hold any entry, the server's own account no longer counts as apart after the upgrade: a log that could back a block in v0.4.1 (Rocky 9 nginx's, say) is judged web_user_writable again. The conditions are in docs/attack-detection-limits.md under "Which web logs can back a block". Default Ubuntu 24.04 and Rocky 9 installs have none of the five directories, so they are not affected (checked on both at 4fcfc52).
  • A correction to v0.4.1's notes: "an address logged in another form (brackets, a port, a zone, leading zeros) is refused" cannot happen through the access logs, which keep only plain addresses. It takes effect only when a log has an IPv4-compatible (::a.b.c.d) or NAT64 (64:ff9b::a.b.c.d) client. The released v0.4.1 entry is left as it was.
  • A Koa handler's context is recognized by how the handler uses it (c.request, c.response, c.state, c.throw, c.assert, or setting c.body, c.status or c.type); any other parameter is read as Express's request. A destructured parameter is read as Express's request, so Koa's ({ request }) => is not followed. Nested patterns ({ headers: { host } }) and string keys ({ 'x-forwarded-host': xfh }) are not followed either; the latter is still reported, by js-ssrf-http-request.
  • Request aliases are kept per function, and an alias reassigned on one branch is no longer followed on any path.
  • @Req() req in a file that does not import NestJS, outside a project that does, is not NestJS's: its req.headers.host is reported by both js-ssrf-host-header and js-ssrf-http-request.
  • The URL check fails closed: global u or nonlocal u anywhere in a file, backslash-continued too, ends it for every u of the file; fetch(u.valueOf()) after a check, and a harmless u['toString'](), are reported.

entry.title: Shentu v0.4.1
entry.content:
• The host survey warns about nginx 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 serving HTTP/2 (a listen ... http2, or http2 on for a server): CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, HTTP/2 memory corruption that lets a client crash the workers. Upgrade to 1.31.9 or 1.30.7, or to the distribution's fixed package; until then, turning HTTP/2 off avoids it. It is advice: the configuration is not changed. A distribution package whose changelog names the CVEs (a backported fix) is not warned about; the package scan reports the distributions' advisories once they reach OSV, and this check covers nginx.org's packages and builds from source, which that scan does not.
  • A web log owned by the server's own account (nginx on Rocky Linux, say) can back a block, as a log root owns can, when nothing else runs as that account: no PHP-FPM pool, systemd unit, crontab, supervisord program, sudo or doas rule or login shell, and at the patrol no process but the server's own; the account databases come only from the files, and everything checked was read. Anything unread leaves the log web_user_writable. The shared default accounts (www-data, apache, nobody) never count. The other conditions are in the limits document, docs/attack-detection-limits.md, under "Which web logs can back a block".
  • nginx's access log sent to journald (access_log syslog:server=unix:/dev/log,...) is read and verified line by line: a line counts only when it came over syslog from nginx's own program, running as nginx's worker account in nginx.service. A line another program sent is read but not verified.
  • shentu log-trust suggest prints the changes that would let this host's web logs back a block: the journald line for nginx, a drop-in lifting journald's rate limit for nginx, kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1, and PHP-FPM pools of their own account. It only prints them and changes nothing.
  • Apache's modules are judged against a list: modules that only configure, control access, cache or proxy are no concern; those that run programs as the children's account, and RewriteMap's prg:, want ptrace_scope 1 or more; mod_php, mod_cgi and unknown modules count as application code.
  • An attack hit in a route placeholder's segment that carries ; parameters (/user/42;x for /user/:id) now reaches L2; before, it stayed at L1.
  • The response-size baseline used for L3 now leaves out only requests taken to L2; requests with hits that are unanchored or noise are learned from.
  • Rule precision: findings that two rules both reported on one line now have one owner (Host header against SSRF, SQL injection, ORDER BY identifiers), and an SSRF host checked against a fixed allowlist on a parsed URL counts as checked. Some findings appear or go away, and with them the routes attack detection takes as reachable.
  • From Telegram, block_ip now blocks only an address with evidence Shentu verified: a verified L2 or L3 attack group listing it, or SSH login events sshd itself logged. Any other address is refused there, to be checked and blocked on the server with shentu chat, as v0.4.0 said of unverified attempts. Before, an address its attack groups did not list (past the ten a group lists, in a group evicted from the state, or logged in another form) was judged by its SSH logins alone, so one with none could be blocked from Telegram on unverified attempts. A group lists at most ten addresses, so the eleventh and later of even a verified L2 or L3 group are refused from Telegram too, by design, and are to be blocked on the server.
  • On the server, an address past the addresses a group lists is refused as a listed one is, also after the group is merged into an overflow summary, and so is the rest of its network. So is an address logged in another form: brackets, a port, a zone, leading zeros (read both ways), or IPv4 embedded in IPv6. A verified group allows a block only of the address it lists. Once an overflow or sink-wide summary has more sources than it keeps hashes of (64), it refuses every address it does not list; the operator may override on the server.
  • v0.4.0's known issue that default nginx logs cannot back a block, planned for v0.4.1, now stands as follows (docs/attack-detection-limits.md has the details): Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 nginx stay web_user_writable (www-data is PHP's account too): send the access log to journald, with ptrace_scope 1. Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 Apache are verified with ptrace_scope 1. Rocky 9 nginx stays web_user_writable, because the default nsswitch.conf also asks sss: taken out (where no SSSD is used), with PHP-FPM as apache, it is verified. Rocky 9 httpd wants ptrace_scope 1, and AllowOverride None everywhere if mod_lua stays loaded.
  • Once a log is judged verified, new attempts go into verified groups, while the old unverified groups expire only after up to 7 days: until then one target may show two groups. A new journald source is read the first time from its latest position on, not from the past.

entry.title: Shentu v0.4.0
entry.content:
• Attack detection (Linux): each patrol round reads the web server's logs and picks out the requests aimed at vulnerabilities this host really has. It alerts; it never blocks on its own. What it cannot see and what it may miss are listed in docs/attack-detection-limits.md.
  • The vulnerability surface: the daily round saves what this host is known to be vulnerable to in state_dir/surface.json, and the other rounds read it: code audit findings, with the routes registering the handler a finding sits in when the same file shows them (#84); advisories of application dependencies and of installed OS packages, compared in dpkg's and rpm's version order; installed WordPress plugins and their versions (#91). A surface missing, unreadable or older than 26 hours is said in the round's notices and the report, never used quietly.
  • Log sources: the access logs nginx and Apache are configured to write, custom formats included, PHP-FPM's logs and journald for application units, read from where the last round stopped across rotation (#85). A log counts as verified only when root alone could have written it; otherwise its attempts are marked unverified and the alert names the reason.
  • 27 attack signatures, written for Shentu or drafted from reviewed nuclei-templates (MIT, see detect/sig/NOTICE), matched after decoding a request at most twice (#87). A request that only reaches a route of a vulnerable handler is L1; one that also carries a payload of the vulnerability's class is L2; L3 needs a sign it had an effect: a response size far from the route's usual one, or an error at the vulnerable file and line (#90). A request cut where it may hide a payload is Unknown. A vulnerability the host does not have is noise.
  • Alerts are the detector's own plain text, sent through the notify channel, not through the model. Attempts are grouped by network (/24 or /64), target and level, and a group is sent once a day. L1 is counted in the daily report, never pushed; Unknown is pushed only when one target gets 20 of them within 24 hours. Sensitive parameters in samples are masked, and the daily file state_dir/reports/attacks-<date>.txt (kept 30 days) masks addresses (#90, #91). shentu detect [--since] [--json] reads and judges a round without sending or saving; the attack_attempts tool and the bot's /attacks list the last day's groups.
  • block_ip and attack detection: an address the detector saw is blocked, after the operator confirms, only for a verified L2 or L3 group of its own. Attempts from unverified logs, at L1 or Unknown, and internal addresses are refused unless the operator overrides with override_unverified on the server (shentu chat); Telegram never can. An address listed only in an overflow summary of many sources is refused, override or not (#91). On an Ubuntu VM, an attack in a verified log was judged L3 and could be blocked; one in an unverified log reached L2 at most, and its block was refused from Telegram.
  • block_ip's SSH evidence counts a login only when sshd's own events in journald confirm it (#91): sshd lines that another program in sshd's own unit writes to journald (for example with logger) no longer back a block; v0.3.1 blocked on them. Lines forged into text logs were refused already.
  • Engine: summary runs that cannot change the result are skipped, and the analysis copies less. Measured as user CPU time on a Mac, WordPress is scanned about 34% faster than v0.3.1 and TypeScript projects about 22% faster, with the same findings (#92). Measured as elapsed time on an Ubuntu 24.04 VM (arm64, 4 CPUs, 4 GB), one version after another on the same machine, the WordPress scan took 97.2 s (v0.3.1 120.0 s, v0.3.0 72.1 s), 19% less than v0.3.1, with the same 2279 files and 43 findings and a peak memory of 848–858 MB in all three; the daily patrol as root took 126 s (v0.3.1 146 s, v0.3.0 99 s). Benchmark unchanged: published vulnerabilities 16 of 97 caught, 1 fixed-release false positive; held-out cases 3 of 30; TypeScript cases 1 of 18 with 1 fixed-release false positive.
  • tools/detecteval, run in CI, measures attack detection on synthetic requests (#94): requests converted from nuclei-templates v10.5.2: a signature of the same class matched 40.5% of them (1548 of 3822 classified templates). This is a match on the request line, not an alert; ordinary requests for 152 routes of 8 applications: 0 false alerts; 363 of them differ in more than tracking parameters, so the rate can only be said to be below about 0.8% (95% upper bound); templates for vulnerabilities the test host has: 3 of 10 alerted, 2 of them only at L1 (the payload is in the request body).
  • When one request hits several rules on the same line of code, you get one alert that lists every rule, instead of one alert per rule (#97).
  • Alerts for a package's CVE no longer carry the note on what routes mean; that note is for alerts about your own code only (#97).
  • When an ACL lets another account write a log or a directory above it, the reason names that account, for example ACL grants write to www-data (uid 33) (#97).
  • When the patrol runs as an account that is not root and not in the systemd-journal or adm group, the SSH result is marked as only partly read (#97).
  • An attack state saved by a v0.4.0 build from before these fixes (one group per rule) is merged into the new format (one group per line of code) when it is loaded (#97, #98). The counts from before the upgrade are a lower bound: when rules of different classes on the same line were hit by different requests, the count may be too low. This changes only the counts shown, not alerts or blocks. v0.3.x keeps no attack state, so an upgrade from it has nothing to merge.
  • Attack detection is for Linux only.
  • Access logs do not record request bodies (POST forms, JSON, uploads): a payload there is never seen, and such a request is L1 at most.
  • The signatures expect the plain form of an attack. Rewritten forms (other encodings, padded paths, comments or other whitespace inside SQL, commands split by quotes) may be missed.
  • With nginx as installed by default on Debian, Ubuntu and Rocky Linux, v0.4.0 judges its access log web_user_writable (the web server's account could write it or a directory above it): its attempts are alerted on, but they cannot back a block. On Debian and Ubuntu nginx and PHP both run as www-data, so the risk is real (on Ubuntu the log is www-data:adm, and logrotate creates it with create 0640 www-data adm). On Rocky Linux nginx runs as nginx and PHP-FPM as apache, which cannot write nginx's log: there v0.4.0 is only being cautious. Changing the log's owner by hand is undone at the next rotation. This is planned for v0.4.1. Rocky Linux's default httpd configuration loads modules outside the list Shentu knows to be safe, so its Apache logs are always judged web_user_writable too; weighing those modules is planned for v0.4.1.
  • There are no signatures for particular WordPress plugin vulnerabilities yet.
  • Scans are still slower than v0.3.0: WordPress about 35% (elapsed time on the Ubuntu VM above), TypeScript projects about 20% (user CPU time on a Mac, #92).
  • Still open from v0.3.1: CVE-2021-23664's fixed release is reported; filesize() on an upload's temporary path in WordPress; markup not followed through a variable.

entry.title: Shentu v0.3.1
entry.content:
• Code audit rules: 70 → 127 (PHP 25 → 51, Python 22 → 43, JavaScript and TypeScript 23 → 33). PHP: WordPress, Laravel, Symfony, Joomla, Drupal, CodeIgniter, Yii and Smarty sinks, sockets and HTTP clients, XML DTDs, template strings, crypto keys and shortcodes (#76). Python: keyword arguments (args=, search_filter=, where=), ldap3 filters and helper flows (#36). JavaScript and TypeScript: Koa and chained Express responses, BSON and launder sanitizers, Host-header redirects and SSRF; .execute( counts only on a receiver that may be a database client (#70).
  • The v0.2.5 known false positives are fixed in the engine: TypeORM repository calls in a file importing typeorm are no MongoDB queries, unless the file uses a MongoDB repository, driver or Mongoose (unless_imports, #59); spawn() and execFile() with shell: true are reported only when the command or its arguments carry input, not the options (several [[args]] blocks per sink, #62); a Server-Sent Events handler (Content-Type: text/event-stream set on every path) is no XSS (unless_content_type, #58; unless_at, #57); ->get_settings() is Elementor widget input only in classes extending \Elementor\Widget_Base (#60); a placeholder list built by array_map with a callback returning a constant is no input (#61); zipfile.ZipFile(request.files[...]) opens the upload's stream, not a path (unless_subscript, #67).
  • js-ssrf-http-request now reads the referrer and origin in Koa, hapi and Fetch API spelling (ctx.request.header.referer, request.headers.referer, request.headers.get('x-callback-url'); not Host), which were missed. Input written into a prepared statement's text is reported once, by php-sqli-prepare-query-text, instead of also by php-sqli-string-concat. The benchmark numbers are unchanged.
  • Engine: new URL(a, base) takes its path and query from a when a starts with / or a scheme (#63); method calls on an object of a class in the same file are followed (#64); an anchored regex test fixing a value's start (re.match(re.escape(base) + r'/[a-z]', url)) is a check for redirect and URL rules (#65); a helper returning a string constant is followed (#66); markup makes an output sink count input only after literal markup (#71); recursive cycles are followed until they settle and paid for once, so WordPress files whose calls were cut went from 48 to 4 (#72); route_input = false for the Host-header rules, and Koa's ctx in the Express model (#50).
  • Survey warns about Apache 2.4.55–2.4.70 with mod_http2 loaded and h2 or h2c in Protocols (CVE-2026-119618; upgrade to 2.4.71, or set Protocols http/1.1 until then) (#54). When a file that could load mod_http2 or turn on h2 cannot be read (no rights, a link not trusted), the check is listed as not checked instead of passed over; the warning says it can be ignored when the distribution has backported the fix.
  • Code audit: a resumed walk cut before its stored position keeps that position, and the position is stored by the root's path; vendor, node_modules and WordPress code folders count only below the site root; wp-content/blogs.dir/*/files and /var/www/<uploads|files> without a site's index are upload folders; authorized_key_unparsed lists the first 20 line numbers (#73).
  • The hourly and daily reports list SSH logins as not checked when the login logs could not be read in full (journald hiding the system's entries from a non-root user, auth.log or secure unreadable, a log cut short). Before, such a run said "nothing new" (#80). The reason given is what kept the logs from counting (on a quiet host: a journal with no sshd entry and no text auth log), and running as root is advised only when rights were missing; on macOS, which keeps sshd's events where Shentu does not read, the report says it has no sshd log source there.
  • Linux builds no longer send an EDNS(0) record with DNS queries, as glibc does not: some DNS servers, VMware's NAT DNS among them, answered such queries without the address, so every lookup (OSV, GitHub) failed with "no such host". When a lookup still fails, the daily report's Not checked line says to check the host's DNS (#80).
  • block_ip refuses an IP whose SSH login events come only from text logs anyone on the host can write to (verified false), or whose logins cannot be read; override_unverified goes ahead after the operator has checked them, from shentu chat only. From the Telegram bot it is always refused, at every confirm level. The check covers SSH login evidence only: a block based on other logs (syslog, nginx, an application log through log_search) is not checked and is the operator's to judge. On a host whose journald has no sshd entries (text logs only), block_ip refuses every IP with SSH login events, whatever the date of the lines; such a block cannot be made from Telegram, only on the server with shentu chat and override_unverified. ssh_logins looks back at most 720 hours, as far as the check (#80). A refusal for login events that may be forged names the text logs they are in.
  • macOS: binary plists count array and dictionary entries, and UTF-16 strings at 9 bytes a character, against the decoding limit; a program path ending in a space is kept as it is; a process named on two ps lines is marked parse_error; periodic_conf_files past 16 files are listed as not read (#80). CI runs go vet and go test on macOS 15 (#81); no macOS binary is published yet.
  • Tests build credential-shaped fake values at run time, so the tree has no secret-shaped literals (#77).
  • Benchmark against v0.3.0: published vulnerabilities 16 of 97 caught (was 15), 1 fixed-release false positive (was 0, see below); held-out cases 3 of 30 (was 2), no fixed-release false positive; TypeScript cases 1 of 18 with 1 fixed-release false positive (n8n), both unchanged.
  • CVE-2021-23664 (@isomorphic-git/cors-proxy): js-ssrf-http-request still reports the fixed release. The proxy forwards req.url after an allow check the engine does not yet read as a sanitizer; reading such checks before a request is planned.
  • Scans take longer with the added rules, as each file is run through more rules: WordPress about 40–60% depending on the machine (on an Ubuntu VM the code audit went from 73.8 s to 120.0 s and the daily patrol from 100 s to 144 s, with the same findings and peak RSS), TypeScript projects about 43%. The fix at the root is planned after v0.3.1.
  • block_ip's check covers SSH login evidence only (see above): a block based on other logs is the operator's to judge.
  • php-deserialization-phar-wrapper still reports filesize() on an upload's temporary path in WordPress's REST attachments controller: the engine cannot yet tell an upload's tmp_name from its client-set name.
  • markup does not follow markup put together in a variable first (const h = '<p>' + x; ctx.body = h).

Rules: 57 added, 0 removed.

entry.title: Shentu v0.3.0
entry.content:
• Windows Server 2022 and 2025, verified on GitHub-hosted windows-2022/2025 runners (amd64; arm64 built too): a Windows collector reads the host through the Windows APIs only (registry, services, processes, sockets, accounts, scheduled tasks, the event log, WMI and the firewall), no PowerShell and no external commands.
  • Windows checks: autostart entries (Run keys, services, scheduled tasks, startup folders, WMI event subscriptions), RDP without NLA, SMB signing and SMBv1, insecure WinRM, firewall profiles, Defender state and exclusions, logon failures and cleared logs.
  • Missing Windows updates against Microsoft's monthly security releases (MSRC), with the CISA KEV list marking the exploited ones first.
  • IIS: web roots from applicationHost.config; the code audit reads ASP and ASP.NET pages and flags webshells and scripts in upload folders, UTF-16 pages included.
  • Two Windows services, Shentu (patrol) and ShentuBot (Telegram), installed with shentu service install [--bot] from %ProgramFiles%\Shentu; configuration and state in %ProgramData%\Shentu, open to SYSTEM and Administrators only.
  • The ssh_logins, processes, accounts_audit and log_search tools work on Windows (logon events, process list, local accounts, event logs).
  • Failed SSH logins are read from journald first: its ssh and sshd units are labelled by journald itself, so a local user cannot forge them. The text logs (auth.log, secure) are read when journald is missing, times out (60 s), or has no sshd entries; anyone on the host can write an sshd line to them with logger, so auth_events is then partial with the new reason unverified_source, and brute-force findings and patrol SSH alerts carry a note saying so. A journal that hides the system's entries from a non-root user is no longer reported as "no failed logins".
  • Amazon Linux 2 and 2023: package vulnerabilities come from Amazon's ALAS advisories (the repositories' updateinfo, checked against the sha256 in repomd.xml and cached), Amazon Linux 2's extras topics included. Amazon Linux 1, past its end of life, answers "cannot tell". Recorded on an Amazon Linux 2023 VM; Amazon Linux 2 is covered by tests only.
  • Alpine Linux: packages from the apk database (OSV), OpenRC services and runlevels, /etc/local.d, busybox crond (/etc/crontabs, /etc/periodic) and /etc/inittab as persistence, and sshd lines of busybox syslog's auth facilities, marked unverified. Recorded on an Alpine 3.22 VM, as root and as a user.
  • SUSE: openSUSE Leap and Tumbleweed, and SLES, SLED and SLES for SAP (one OSV ecosystem per SLE 15 module; the ones OSV does not carry are listed as not queried). Leap is tested with a synthetic fixture and SLES on no real host yet.
  • The daily report says when a vulnerability check failed or covered only part, and a package list that parsed to nothing is "cannot tell" instead of "no vulnerabilities".
  • macOS (new, read-only, never with sudo): platform, accounts (dscl), processes, listeners (netstat, or lsof when macOS hides sockets), the application firewall, SIP, Gatekeeper, FileVault, XProtect, launchd jobs and other persistence, sshd settings, and installed apps and Homebrew packages. The OS version is checked against Apple's software update catalog (gdmf.apple.com); packages answer "cannot tell", since OSV has no Homebrew ecosystem. Tested only with a synthetic fixture (an invented host); not yet verified on a real Mac. Login items are not parsed (the Background Task Management store), so macOS persistence is always partial. periodic.conf and daily/weekly/monthly.local are listed line by line, every line but blanks and plain comments (a # line with no quote, $ or backtick: in a heredoc such a line is data and runs its commands); they are short. A stock /etc/defaults/periodic.conf is left out, and the files periodic_conf_files names are read too.
  • A code audit root written with a trailing slash (/var/www/html/) or as / is no longer skipped when an audit resumes inside it. Roots are now cleaned, so the first audit after the upgrade does not find the place the last one stopped and walks from the start once.
  • sshd settings: a Match block inside an included file (Include sshd_config.d/*.conf) no longer hides the settings that follow the Include in the main file (sshd restores the Match state after each Include), so e.g. a later PermitRootLogin yes is reported. An Include nested more than 4 deep, or past 256 config files, is listed as unread.
  • Building from source now needs Go 1.26 or later (was 1.23): the Windows collector uses golang.org/x/sys, the second dependency.
  • Windows is read-only: block_ip and unblock_ip are not supported there.
  • Windows Server 2019 is best effort: expected to work (the same Windows APIs, build 17763) but not verified on GitHub-hosted runners (they offer no 2019 image).
  • shentu setup does not run on Windows yet; the configuration is written by hand.
  • The Windows binary is not code-signed and there is no MSI; SmartScreen or an antivirus may warn about it.

entry.title: Shentu v0.2.5
entry.content:
• app_code_audit follows calls across files: input read in one file and used in a sink of another is reported at the sink, with the file it came from.
  • Framework route models: the parameters of WordPress hooks, shortcodes and REST routes, Laravel routes, Django URLs, Flask and FastAPI views and Express handlers are input, also when the route is registered in another file.
  • New rule classes: LDAP injection, NoSQL operator injection, dangerous file uploads, weak cryptography and hard-coded credentials; TypeScript files are checked with the JavaScript rules.
  • Audits keep their results between runs, so a large application is covered over a few patrols instead of one.
  • The audit sizes itself to the server: heap at most min(1 GiB, 25% of available memory, 50% of the service's cgroup), workers from the CPU count and the load.
  • Fewer false positives: wp_send_json output, JSON_HEX_TAG data blocks, MongoDB queries on objects that are not collections, and Django _meta.get_field checks.
  • An audit spread over several runs can still report a few findings that differ from one run without a time limit; a fix is in progress.
  • php-deserialization-phar-wrapper reports filesize() on an upload's temporary path in WordPress's REST attachments controller, a false positive: the path is PHP's own, but the engine cannot yet tell an upload's tmp_name from its client-set name.
  • js-nosqli-mongo-query reports TypeORM repository calls on SQL databases (find/findOne whose options hold a where built from request values, e.g. n8n's public API and credential lookups) as MongoDB queries; TypeORM sends those values as SQL parameters, so these are false positives, to be told apart by a TypeORM-aware receiver check in v0.2.6.
  • js-cmdi-spawn-shell still reports spawn() and execFile() calls whose command and arguments are fixed when only the options (such as cwd or env) carry request values.
  • js-xss-response has no Server-Sent Events exception: res.write("data: " + value) in a text/event-stream handler is reported as XSS (a false positive), and nothing is missed because of SSE; telling streams apart by the handler's Content-Type is planned for v0.2.6.
  • ->get_settings() counts as Elementor widget input in every class, so WP_Widget::get_settings() and WooCommerce WC_Settings_Page::get_settings() values (saved by administrators) are reported too. Limiting the source to classes extending \Elementor\Widget_Base needs class-scoped sources in the engine (planned for v0.2.6). Values read through ->get_settings() can also be followed into WordPress admin field definitions and into a few SQL sinks that are already guarded (an isset() check, or a value bound through $wpdb->prepare() inside ORDER BY FIELD()), which gives extra false positives there. Narrowing the source to Elementor widgets is planned for v0.2.6.
  • In $wpdb->prepare()/->prepare() formats, a placeholder list built by a callback that returns a constant (implode(',', array_map(fn($v) => '%d', $ids)), or the same with function ($v) { return '%d'; }) is still treated as input and reported when $ids comes from the request. array_fill(0, count($ids), '%d') and sizeof() are recognised. Reading a callback's return value needs an engine change (planned for v0.2.6).
  • python-path-traversal-send-file reports zipfile.ZipFile(request.files[...]), which opens the uploaded stream rather than a path, a false positive. Telling a request's file stream from a client-set file name inside one argument needs an engine change (planned for v0.2.6).

Rules: 37 added, 0 removed.
